projectDesc.p: The digital part of the SNSF project 'Caroline Spurgeon: Chaucer Allusions, Shakespeare's Imagery, and the Digital Humanities' aims to create the first open-access database dedicated to the criticism and reception of Chaucer throughout history. It draws on the compilation and cataloguing work carried out by Professor Caroline Spurgeon (1869–1942) and collected in 'Five Hundred Years of Chaucer Criticism and Allusion'. This work consists of three volumes and a supplement, which will be systematically transcribed, corrected, enriched, encoded and published online, in order to facilitate future research and bring new perspectives to light.

editorialDecl.p: The original spelling and punctuation are retained. Meaningful layouts are reproduced, i.e. verses, printed marginalia, dots lines, tables, etc. However, we do not consider, the line breaks for prose, the columns or the curly brackets. The same rules apply for special characters and glyphs. Otiose letters are normalised, as well as spaces before punctuation marks.

div.ab: 1900. Schofield, William Henry. Chaucer's Franklin's Tale, [in] Publications Modern Language Assn. of America, Baltimore, 1901, vol. xvi (new series, ix), pp. xxxvii, 405-49.

ab.seg: [General description of the Franklin's Tale, with the point that the story of Arviragus is given in the Historia Regum Britanniœ of Geoffrey of Monmouth, before the time of Marie de France, and suggestions as to how this fictitious history got built up. The third part of the paper closely examines the phraseology, incidents, and sentiments of Chaucer's narrative in order to detect how much his version owes to the probable Breton source. The conclusion is: 'We surely need no more evidence from the poems of Marie de France... It must now be clear that the Franklin's Tale, not only in fundamental theme, but also in minute de- tail, shows so great similarity to the extant Breton lays that there can be no doubt that Chaucer's assertion regarding the source of his narrative is to be unhesitatingly accepted..." (p. 432). The fourth part discusses the oriental parallels to part of the story, and shows that these do not destroy the possibility of its source being a Breton lay, such lays being a very mixed product. Studies of other romances form part of the evidence. The fifth part of the paper discusses Chaucer's handling of the theme and claims original work by him in connexion with four developments: 1. The discussion of the cause of evil in the world, à propos of the existence of the dangerous rocks on the Breton coast. 2. Astrological references. 3. The 'pleynt' of Aurelius to Apollo (303-51). 4. Dorigen's 'compleynt' to Fortune (627-728).]
